In DGBL environments, learners interact with computer-based games where educational content is embedded within gaming scenarios, guiding learners to accomplish tasks through exploration, decision-making and problem-solving (Poompimol et al. 2024; Prensky 2007). These games are often designed to create immersive learning experiences by offering challenges that foster cognitive development and skill acquisition, with the support of instant feedback mechanisms that promote reflection and revision (Kinzie and Joseph 2008; Oblinger 2004). Learners are typically required to complete missions or solve problems that align with educational goals,
expectedSources.paper-02-s-acadcc7eff07: encouraging both enjoyment and deep learning (Cagiltay 2007; Coller and Scott 2009). Due to its interactive and engaging nature, DGBL has been applied in various educational contexts such as mathematics, language learning, science and vocational training (Liu and Chu 2010).

expectedSources.paper-02-s-ea1bc34a3c6f: This digital game system is designed around a learning unit focused on animal habitats and their associated environmental characteristics. As shown in Figure 2, the gameplay begins with the initiation of the game and presentation of scene-specific information. Students then answer quiz questions based on the habitat content. Based on their responses, the system provides immediate feedback indicating whether their answers are correct or incorrect, followed by the opportunity to collect badges as a reward. During the gaming process, the system also includes opportunities for students to retry missions, identify correct and incorrect information and receive final explanations. In the later stages, students
expectedSources.paper-02-s-8a7534145456: review what they have learned through system feedback and then engage in a concept map review and reflection stage, where they view and organise the integrated concept map to consolidate their understanding. This indicates that students sometimes proceeded to answer tasks after reviewing knowledge content. Given that the CM-CLDG model involved concept maps as a guiding framework, it is possible that students engaged in review for purposes beyond immediate answering, such as identifying concept gaps or updating their understanding through the concept map. expectedSources.paper-02-s-529ee340799b: Analysis showed no significant difference in learning anxiety between the CM-CLDG and C-CLDG groups. This may be due
expectedSources.paper-02-s-45e8bcdc3b35: to the students' previous exposure to digital learning, which could have normalised the game-based environment and reduced potential anxiety triggers. Although prior research has found that concept maps may alleviate language anxiety by providing clearer structures and reducing ambiguity (Chen and Hwang 2020), the already moderate anxiety levels observed in this study may have limited the potential for measurable differences. Future studies may consider applying similar interventions in higher-anxiety contexts to better assess the affective benefits of concept mapping. Krashen's affective filter hypothesis (1982) suggests that anxiety influences language acquisition by either facilitating or impeding input processing. In this study, the relatively low affective filter across both groups may have reduced the observable impact of concept mapping on anxiety reduction.

additions.sourceText: In physical education (PE), students’ movement skills performance serves as a key indicator for assessing teaching effectiveness. Enhancing students’ movement skills requires fostering their understanding of relevant theoretical knowledge and ensuring their proper execution of movements. Additionally, it is imperative to minimize incorrect practice to prevent potential sports injuries and declines in performance, ultimately achieving the educational goal of skill improvement. However, providing personalized guidance tailored to each student’s individual needs presents significant challenges for teachers (Chao et al., 2021; Yan & Cardinal, 2013; Yan & FitzPatrick, 2016). As a consequence, scholars have introduced technology-assisted learning, which has successfully demonstrated its effectiveness in terms of supporting PE courses (Almusawi et al., 2021; Moon et al., 2023). In particular, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) has opened up more opportunities for technology-assisted learning and personalized guidance (Chen et al., 2022; Lai & Tu, 2024; Tu & Lu, 2025). For example, AI speech recognition technology can instantly translate and assist students in learning languages (Darvishi et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). Motion capture technology can analyze students’ movement skills performance and provide personalized guidance based on individual learning progress and challenges (Hsia et al., 2024, 2025; Li et al., 2024; Song, 2024). These studies have indicated that the personalized feedback provided by AI can indeed help most students learn more efficiently. However, some students have reported difficulties in understanding the learning performance analysis provided by AI, suggesting that they require additional support to fully comprehend their issues (Liu et al., 2024; Song, 2024; Wang et al., 2023). To address this issue, some scholars have suggested providing a visualized learning analytics dashboard that presents key indicators through simple charts, helping students understand and reflect on their learning process (Lee & Kim, 2024). In line with this recommendation, this study presented assessment results in a visualized format to assist students in overcoming language barriers and in understanding movement skills guidance.

expectedSources.paper-04-s-36e5b8f7b1d5: Guided by these frameworks, the semester was structured into three phases (Figure 1). The first phase (Weeks 1–9) focused on theoretical foundations through lectures and discussions on health promotion principles, behaviour theories, and global strategies. The second (Weeks 10–11) developed planning skills through needs assessments and intervention design. The final phase (Weeks 12–18) centred on co-creative application, where students worked in groups of 6–7 to design educational board games for elementary students. Each group selected a specific health theme (e.g. balanced diet, infectious disease prevention, air pollution prevention), conducted audience analysis, defined learning objectives, and created
expectedSources.paper-04-s-d74d614c077b: game mechanics and storylines to communicate health messages. Weekly workshops and consultations supported prototype development, peer playtesting, and iterative refinement, concluding with a public presentation that connected theory to community practice.

One student noted, ‘Designing a game made me realise how difficult it is to simplify complex health messages’. Several students expressed that the task deepened their understanding as it required them to translate theoretical content into child-friendly formats. expectedSources.paper-05-s-184f03e51f7d: Collaborative learning has been recognized as an important and effective approach to fostering students’ higher order thinking as well as their collaboration and communication competences (Markula & Aksela, 2022; Quines, 2017; Rorimpandey et al., 2022). In the past decades, several previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of engaging students in collaborative learning tasks (Knoche, 2022; Suendarti & Virgana, 2022). For example, in a reading and writing course, Marcos et al. (2020) employed cooperative learning to encourage students to collaboratively analyze and write in groups and develop their own perspectives, and found that this approach effectively enhanced their creative thinking. However, research has indicated that when students engage in group-based problem-solving tasks without sufficient guidance or support, they may feel confused or even experience anxiety during the
expectedSources.paper-05-s-3d191ecf127b: learning process (Tsai & Wu, 2021). When conducting conventional collaborative learning activities, teachers often manage numerous students and groups, making it difficult to adequately address the needs of each group. As indicated by several scholars, collaborative learning facilitates social negotiation and shared knowledge construction; however, it may lack sufficient structure without appropriate scaffolding (Kokku et al., 2018; Tsai & Wu, 2021); that is, providing timely guidance or immediate feedback or guidance to individual collaborative learning groups remains a critical challenge in educational contexts (Hsu et al., 2023; Kokku et al., 2018; Tsai & Wu, 2021).

expectedSources.paper-05-s-ec011b729eea: In the field of education, collaborative learning has been widely applied and is regarded as an effective instructional strategy for enhancing student learning (Gillies, 2003; Hron & Friedrich, 2003; Kokku et al., 2018). Several researchers have revealed that collaborative learning can significantly improve students’ academic performance (Rorimpandey et al., 2022; Suendarti & Virgana, 2022), collective efficacy (Gillies, 2019), critical thinking tendencies (Huang et al., 2017; Quines, 2017), as well as problem-solving and decision-making abilities (Knoche, 2022). These benefits can also be explained by Social Cognitive Theory, which emphasizes that learning occurs through social interaction and observational processes within a shared environment (Bandura, 1986, 2000). Building upon the foundations of collaborative learning, PBL has emerged as a structured approach that embodies its core principles. It is commonly regarded as a concrete form of collaborative learning, and is deeply inspired by the theory of social constructivism (Vygotsky, 1986). According to Vygotsky’s (1986) view of social constructivism, knowledge is constructed through social interaction, language communication, and collaborative activities in cultural contexts. In a PBL context, students discuss, reason, and share knowledge about real problems in small groups, and develop understanding and solutions through peer collaboration and reflection
expectedSources.paper-05-s-db9e4a1c675f: (Markula & Aksela, 2022; Tsai & Wu, 2021). This learning process strengthens learners’ active participation and realizes the key role of social interaction in cognitive development and knowledge construction.Krajcik and Shin’s (2014) framework of the key characteristics of PBL divides collaborative learning into different stages, namely a driving question, learning goals, scientific practices, collaboration, using technological tools, and creating an artefact, which help to enhance students’ problem-solving skills. Previous research has shown that engaging students in collaborative learning and PBL tasks can enhance not only their academic achievement but also their group self-efficacy, critical thinking tendencies, and problem-solving skills (Huang et al., 2017; Knoche, 2022; Ma et al., 2023).

expectedSources.paper-05-s-00f5cde595f5: Lastly, we propose the following recommendations to guide future research in exploring the challenges and potential of AI tools in education:
expectedSources.paper-05-s-ea2f8fcf220d: 1. It is recommended that future research explore how to integrate GAI with other personalized learning systems or to develop further personalized AI models that can automatically adjust content and teaching methods based on students’ learning situations and performance, thereby enhancing the educational applicability of AI tools. In this context, concept mapping can be incorporated as a visual and diagnostic tool to represent students’ cognitive structures, enabling the AI system to better identify learning gaps and tailor instructional prompts accordingly. 2. Future research should integrate GAI with various teaching modes, using it as a supplementary tool rather than as the primary learning pathway. Educators could combine AI technology with conventional teaching methods to foster collaboration and discussion between teachers and students, thereby balancing the importance of technological applications with interpersonal communication. 3. The convenience of immediate feedback provided by GAI may reduce opportunities for students to engage in independent thinking. If students become accustomed to relying on GAI for answers, they may neglect the underlying logical reasoning and analytical processes, potentially leading to a decline in their cognitive abilities. Therefore, it is recommended that future educators design challenging tasks that require students to reflect, summarize, and critique after using AI. For instance, students could be asked to further explain or expand upon the AI-generated answers, ensuring that they not only understand the results but also grasp the underlying processes and principles. 4. Since GAI’s responses are based on existing data and patterns, it may not be effective in terms of fostering students’ creative thinking, particularly in situations that require divergent thinking or innovative problem solving. Future research could explore how to integrate GAI with creative learning activities, such as designing tasks that ask students to critique or expand on AIgenerated answers, thereby stimulating their creative thinking. Additionally, teachers could use GAI to generate different options or perspectives, prompting students to engage in assessments, make comparisons, and express their creativity. 5. It is also crucial to consider ethical issues, including AI bias, misinformation, and student data privacy. 6. In addition, exploring the role of teacher facilitation, cooperative learning dimensions, and the relationship between affective and metacognitive constructs may further enhance the educational effectiveness of AI-assisted learning.

expectedSources.paper-07-s-1ff4ed8310b3: Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education is widely recognised as a crucial approach for enhancing students' scientific literacy, critical thinking, and abilities
expectedSources.paper-07-s-4be57cc5ce09: to solve interdisciplinary problems (English 2023). Integrating science, technology, engineering, and mathematics into real-world scenarios, STEM education fosters students' autonomous exploration and innovative practises, deepening their disciplinary knowledge and honing their problem-solving skills
expectedSources.paper-07-s-20ce8776f777: (Tan et al. 2023). As educational technologies evolve, the importance of STEM education has become more prominent in the educational sector (Li et al. 2020). Yet, its practical application encounters numerous challenges, such as the abstract nature of scientific knowledge (Qian and Choi 2023), the complexity of learning materials (Gao et al. 2020), and traditional teaching methods falling short when it comes to motivating students intrinsically, thus limiting their learning motivation and effectiveness (Lin and Wang 2021). From a cognitive science perspective, these challenges can impose a high cognitive load on students, hindering their ability to effectively process information and engage in deep learning (Sweller 1994). The question of how to effectively create realistic learning environments that enable students to comprehend and apply abstract and complex concepts is now a central concern in educational research and practise (Chernikova et al. 2020).

expectedSources.paper-07-s-e3d5d0b0eb45: Alternate Reality Games (ARGs) are interactive narratives that use the real world as a platform, often blurring the line between the game and reality (Örnebring 2007). Unlike typical games that are confined to a screen, ARGs integrate digital content with real-world locations and tasks to create an immersive, trans-media experience (Jagoda et al. 2015). Grounded in situated learning theory, they are extensively employed to kindle students' passion for learning and to promote their active engagement (Gilliam et al. 2017; Meekaew and Ketpichainarong 2021). Through the creation of puzzles and challenges, ARGs effectively boost students' motivation to learn (Hou et al. 2023; Sofianidis et al. 2024) and facilitate their problem-solving in blended virtual and real settings (Stylianidou et al. 2020). Although ARGs are widely recognised for their significant potential to foster active inquiry, research indicates that many students struggle with the organisation and processing of complex real-world information, which impacts their performance in ARG tasks (Whitton et al. 2014). For example, the overload of multimodal information, including
expectedSources.paper-07-s-17594c7f3b22: visual, auditory, and textual data, can increase cognitive load, thereby reducing students' efficiency of information processing (Moon and Ryu 2021). To unlock the full potential of ARGs in STEM education, it is vital to provide tailored learning support that assists students in navigating challenges encountered during the inquiry process, thus boosting their inquiry skills and educational outcomes (Liang et al. 2021).

expectedSources.paper-07-s-83df2fb4775c: Despite their potential, students encounter numerous challenges during the learning process in ARGs. The inherent uncertainty of puzzles in ARGs, coupled with the complexities of real-world scenarios, heightens the difficulty of problem solving, often impeding students' ability to collect clues and synthesise information for task completion (Gilliam et al. 2017). Throughout the ARG tasks, students may feel frustrated, discouraged, and distracted, which can prevent them from achieving the desired learning outcomes. Some may lose motivation altogether if the challenges surpass their abilities (Richey et al. 2019). Given the complexity and diversity of these tasks, ineffective organisation and internalisation of information can disrupt students' cognitive construction processes (Glazewski and Ertmer 2020). Furthermore, an overload of tasks or information can lead to cognitive overload, undermining the efficiency and effectiveness of their knowledge construction (Sewell et al. 2020; Xu and Ouyang 2022). Successfully navigating these challenges requires learners to possess strong metacognitive skills to monitor their understanding, manage cognitive load, and adjust their problem-solving strategies (Seufert 2018). However, students
expectedSources.paper-07-s-e0ff821cb8e9: often struggle to self-regulate effectively in such complex environments (Jin et al. 2023). This highlights a critical need for adaptive, personalised feedback within ARGs to serve as an external scaffold, thereby fostering the metacognitive awareness necessary for successful inquiry-based learning.

expectedSources.paper-07-s-4aa3140070c7: Figure 2 illustrates the ARG system workflow, where students engage in learning and complete all ARG tasks with the assistance and support of the virtual agent, ‘V.’ The system includes four game tasks: ‘Accepting the Invitation,’ ‘Kart Structure,’ ‘Three
expectedSources.paper-07-s-c2526d3d23fa: Electrical Systems,’ and ‘Four Key Processes,’ each mapped to a planned learning pathway for students. After completing one task, students can proceed to the next or choose to review previous content. Upon entering a task, students explore the scene to learn relevant knowledge points and collect knowledge cards through their exploration. They are also required to complete test questions to achieve the task objectives. Additionally, students can review their acquired knowledge cards and game achievements in the Library and Achievement Gallery sections on the home page, further reinforcing their learning outcomes.

Finally, the mathematics dimension emphasises the development of quantitative analysis skills by engaging students in tasks such as measuring component dimensions, calculating speed-to-weight ratios, and applying geometric principles to enhance kart performance.

expectedSources.paper-07-s-4520fa7115b4: The LLM-ARG system is composed of four core modules. The first module is Students Interacting with Agent ‘V’. In this module,
expectedSources.paper-07-s-8bced326db9b: students interact with the virtual agent through various inputs, including player input, variable identification, instruction understanding, and persona dialogue. expectedSources.paper-07-s-24c5148c840d: The second module is Data Processing and Transmission, which handles data interaction between the game environment and
expectedSources.paper-07-s-47df2253ccf0: the Baidu AI Cloud Qianfan Platform. It consists of three key components: Call Plugin, Data Transmission, and Parsing Data Plugin. The Call Plugin manages obtaining Access Tokens and submitting HTTP requests to the Qianfan platform for model invocation. The Data Transmission component processes prompt data and game data to facilitate real-time interaction between the game engine and the large model. The Parsing Data Plugin is responsible for extracting and processing dialogue content from the model output, ensuring that the feedback provided by ‘V’ is relevant and coherent.

expectedSources.paper-07-s-4d60846e66a6: The experimental group received real-time feedback through the LLM-ARG system, including knowledge-based feedback, task-oriented feedback, and achievement-driven motivational feedback. Knowledge-based feedback was designed to reinforce learned content, task-oriented feedback supported the construction of cognitive structures, and achievement-based feedback motivated students by rewarding their progress with achievements and items. In contrast, the control group's C-ARG system employed a traditional rule-based e-learning approach. The agent's feedback was limited to pre-scripted responses triggered by predefined rules (e.g., confirming a correct answer or providing a generic hint after an incorrect one). Crucially, this system lacked the LLM's capacity for
expectedSources.paper-07-s-d18dd0735edb: dynamic, conversational interaction; it could not interpret student-initiated questions in natural language, diagnose the underlying nature of a misconception, or provide personalised metacognitive prompts. This design allows for a direct comparison between a standard game-based learning environment with basic feedback and one enhanced with novel LLM-driven, dialogic scaffolding, which is the focus of our study.

expectedSources.paper-07-s-1254fae764b4: In Week 1, learners engaged in introductory activities, which began with a 20-min session to introduce learning activities and rules. Following this, students completed a 30-min pretest to assess academic performance and metacognitive awareness. These introductory activities ensured that all participants had a clear understanding of the learning objectives and initial baseline data before engaging in the main instructional content. During Weeks 2 to 4, both the experimental group and the control group participated in core instructional activities designed to build STEM knowledge and skills through lectures and hands-on problem-solving tasks. Following the instructional activities, each group completed a 60-min ARG task independently. The LLM-ARG group interacted with the personalised virtual agent ‘V’, which provided adaptive, real-time support, whilst the C-ARG group followed the same instructional activities using a system that provided only traditional, non-adaptive guidance, the specifics of which are detailed in the Participants section. Both groups were exposed to identical scenarios, educational content, and task durations to ensure consistency in the learning environment. In Week 5, a 60-min posttest was conducted to evaluate academic performance and post-intervention metacognitive awareness. This design ensured that the ARG intervention was systematically integrated into the
expectedSources.paper-07-s-beabcea471ec: standard curriculum, maintaining consistent instructional time and task structure for both groups.

expectedSources.paper-07-s-55befeabff99: This study employed ANCOVA to investigate the differences in the metacognitive awareness scores of the experimental and control groups. The instructional method was designated as the independent variable, with post-questionnaire metacognitive awareness scores serving as the dependent variable and pre-questionnaire scores as the covariate. The Levene's test for equality of variances did not reach statistical significance (F = 1.932, p = 0.170), confirming the assumption of homogeneity of variances. The test for homogeneity of regression coefficients indicated no significant interaction between the groups and the pretest scores (p = 0.554), demonstrating that the data met the fundamental assumptions of ANCOVA. Table 4 presents the descriptive statistics for both
expectedSources.paper-07-s-9a8098b194be: groups. After accounting for the pretest scores, ANCOVA revealed a significant difference in the scores of the two groups (F = 4.480, p = 0.039). According to Ferguson (2009), a partial η2 of 0.077 indicates a small effect size. This suggests that students using the LLM-ARG significantly outperformed those using C-ARG in terms of metacognitive awareness, indicating that the LLM-based virtual agent ARG enhanced students' metacognitive awareness.

additions.sourceText: In the VR scenario, learners were guided to engage in self-explanation based on systematic guiding questions to facilitate reflection and knowledge organisation, thereby deepening their understanding and construction of the learning content. Across the four stages of the model, self-explanation serves as a bridge between individual sense-making and subsequent social knowledge co-construction, ensuring that learners enter collaborative phases with cognitively prepared and explicit representations. The model consists of four stages, as shown in Figure 1. Each stage operationalises a distinct regulatory function, progressively guiding learners from unstructured exploration towards coordinated collaborative knowledge construction. The following sections explicitly highlight the logical progression between stages and how cognitive readiness established in earlier stages lays the foundation for subsequent phases.

Construction stage: A learning activity that involved exploration and self-explanation of the virtual museum. First, learners actively explored the background knowledge of the artefacts through structured guiding questions embedded in each scene of the virtual museum. The system provided real-time interactive feedback to assist learners in initially checking their understanding. These guiding questions also prompted learners to think about how new knowledge was organised and how it linked to their previous experiences. Through feedback from the system, learners were able to review the correctness of the knowledge content and actively construct knowledge instead of passively accepting information (Figure 3). Notably, the structured guiding questions provided real-time feedback so that learners could secure an accurate initial grasp of the artefacts' factual information. Afterwards, the self-explanation task asked learners to digest, organise, and internalise these verified ideas. Learners constructed coherent meaning in their own words. By design, this task offered no instant system feedback; its aim was to foster an individual generative cognitive process.

Next, in order to deepen knowledge construction, this study adopted the self-explanation-guided virtual museum learning model, which allowed learners to complete self-explanation tasks in textual form through online structured guiding worksheets (Figure 4). The core of the self-explanation strategy was to motivate learners to externalise their own understanding of knowledge, which not only reduced the burden on their working memory but also enhanced their participation in the construction of meaning in the content, generating clear and detailed descriptions of knowledge for themselves. Specifically, this process required learners to organise and reorganise content, making meaningful connections between new information and existing knowledge. In this study, “connecting existing information with new concepts” was operationalised through artefact appreciation. Students already possessed fragmented understandings from class and supplements, for instance, knowledge of dynasty context and social customs (e.g., the Tang dynasty's emphasis on burial items), the symbolism of idioms (e.g., 螽斯衍慶, denoting many descendants), and the evolution of scripts and inscriptions (e.g., text cast on the inner walls of bronze vessels). In virtual museum learning, learners were situated in an artefact appreciation context. They activated and reorganised their prior knowledge and then integrated it with new, artefact-specific information via self-explanation tasks. The process of translating understanding into words facilitated learners’ knowledge construction, and enhanced the retention and subsequent transfer of knowledge.

Collaboration stage: Group members constructed a concept map of knowledge through synchronous collaboration, shared the results of their group discussions (Figure 5), presented their work to the class, and received feedback and suggestions from both peers and the teacher. The collaborative process not only required members to organise and connect the core concepts together but also facilitated the externalisation and sharing of knowledge through visual images. Through collaborative planning and practice, group members achieved collaborative knowledge construction and deepened their systematic understanding of the content. Collaborative knowledge construction at this stage benefited from the refined understanding and clarification achieved during the conversation stage. Through the scaffolding provided by the preceding construction and conversation stages, learners entered the collaboration phase with sufficient cognitive readiness and a shared foundation of understanding. This enabled the final collaborative concept mapping to proceed efficiently.

Students mentioned several advantages that promote learning effectiveness. These included focusing on understanding the learning content, reviewing and reflecting on the learning content, and enhancing interdisciplinary knowledge. Besides, the experimental group specifically reported one benefit: strengthening impressive understanding of knowledge (Table 8).
2. Fostering Critical Thinking

Students reported that the learning process fostered critical thinking. This included the ability to promote diverse thinking. Besides, the experimental group uniquely reported two abilities: evaluating the accuracy of viewpoints and developing independent thinking skills (Table 8). Most students in the experimental group stated that before participating in facilitating collaboration, they built their understanding and perspectives on the content through the process of self-explanation, which involved developing independent thinking skills. This process helped them more effectively evaluate the accuracy of viewpoints during group collaboration and provide constructive feedback.
3. Fostering Collaboration

In terms of facilitating collaboration, students mentioned several aspects. These included the ability to communicate and share opinions, as well as the ability to collaborate to complete tasks. Besides, the experimental group additionally reported an extra ability: achieving group consensus (Table 8). Most students in the experimental group believed that after completing the self-explanation task, they could express their viewpoints more clearly when entering group discussions. Through communicating and sharing opinions, they were able to compare and integrate different ideas, which helped them achieve group consensus. In contrast, students in the control group often mentioned situations where they either omitted certain content or struggled to explain their thoughts clearly.
4. Enhancing Metacognition

In terms of enhancing metacognition, students mentioned the ability to develop and refine conceptual knowledge. Besides, the experimental group solely reported two abilities: self-monitoring comprehension and adapting learning strategies (Table 8). Most students in the experimental group stated that when answering the self-explanation task questions, they were better able to monitor their understanding of the learning content. They also became more aware of the information easily overlooked during the exploration of the virtual museum scenes, prompting them to adapt their learning strategies and focus more on the key information.
5. Increasing Learning Motivation

In terms of increasing learning motivation, students reported two common willingness indicators: their willingness to apply the approach to other courses and their willingness to continue to use the approach. Besides, the experimental group exclusively reported an additional aspect: the desire to explore the learning content further (Table 8). E04 stated that this learning approach sparked their interest in learning and made them curious about the interdisciplinary knowledge embedded in the artefacts. It also motivated them to proactively read the learning materials first whenever entering a new scene. C05 expressed that the learning method was very interesting, and they hoped to continue using it and apply it to different course content. Besides, E08 mentioned that the museum collections contain many artefacts, but this learning activity only focused on a few items. After completing the collaborative concept mapping with the group, E08 expressed the hope to have more opportunities to explore additional artefacts in the future.
